title: Biohazard and trauma cleaning
estimatedMinutesNote: Estimated, not verified. Rule: learner text 3858 words / 100 per minute + 3 min per knowledge check (12) + 5 min allowance, rounded to nearest 5, minimum 15.

instruction.heading: Module authority and restricted work
instruction.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to enter, assess, clean, decontaminate, release, transport or dispose of anything at a scene or in any regulated setting. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate, clearance or permission to do restricted work. Some of the work described here is restricted to licensed, authorised or specially trained people, and some of it may not be done by a general cleaner at all. Where legal, police, coronial, insurer, property-owner or occupational-health authority applies, that authority must be obtained and recorded before any step is taken. Nothing in this lesson replaces the employer's written procedure, the site-specific assessment or the decision of the competent, authorised party. Where you cannot identify who holds that authority, the answer is to stop and refer.

instruction.heading: 1. Professional scope and restricted-work triage
instruction.body: Routine cleaning and trauma remediation are different jobs with different safety, legal, insurance and waste conditions. The coordinator must tell them apart before a quote is given or a worker is assigned. A client's description, such as 'just a deep clean' after a serious incident, cannot establish what material is present, so treat it as an unverified enquiry. Before going further, confirm access permission, release by the responsible authority, the business's insurance position, the training held by the people who would attend, and the local waste rules. Write down every unknown, because an unknown is a reason to pause, not a reason to proceed. Before any practical operation, identify the authorised scope, the responsible supervisor, the site assessment, the local requirements and the employer's written procedure. Generic examples in this course do not replace any of those. Your decision record should name the approver, the source documents, the boundaries of the work, the unresolved risks and the person who receives the handover.

instruction.heading: 2. Pathogen and exposure risk fundamentals
instruction.body: Biological hazards can be visible, such as a spill, or concealed in porous materials, narrow gaps, equipment and waste. Workers do not identify a pathogen by looking at it, and unknown body fluids and sharps may carry infectious risk whatever they appear to be. Uncertainty is a reason to pause and obtain a professional assessment. It is never evidence that the area is safe. The main exposure routes to consider are contact with broken skin, splashes to the eyes, nose or mouth, puncture from sharps, and, where aerosols or dust are produced, inhalation. A photograph does not show whether residue has reached carpet underlay, timber joints or the space behind a wall, so appearance cannot be used to infer clearance. Review the employer's exposure-control plan and confirm that the tasks match each worker's training and any vaccination or occupational-health requirements that apply. Build a hazard inventory that lists each exposure route, the uncertainty attached to it, who assesses it and who owns the escalation.

instruction.heading: 3. Scene entry permissions and site isolation
instruction.body: A trauma-related worksite can involve several parties with different interests, including police, the property manager or landlord, the insurer, next of kin and the occupants. Permission from one of them does not necessarily amount to release by all the authorities that need to agree. Before any entry is considered, confirm in writing who controls the site, who has released it, what the entry conditions are and who is responsible for the entry log. Plan for privacy protection, controlled entry, welfare of people nearby, communications and the segregation of the public from any potentially contaminated area. A neighbour who offers to let a contractor into a sealed property is not a source of authority. Missing from that offer are the written authorisation of the responsible party, the release by the authority controlling the site, the insurer's position, a documented hazard assessment and an entry log. In training, draft an entry-authorisation checklist and a communication chain, but do not simulate entry into a real affected scene.

instruction.heading: 4. Sharps and concealed hazards recognition
instruction.body: Needles, broken glass and concealed debris are hazards in their own right. Do not search for concealed sharps by hand, do not sort through debris to find them and do not move unidentified objects to speed up the work. Sharps hazards need trained personnel, approved equipment, a specified collection process and local disposal arrangements. If a sharp is found, stop, keep people out of the area, do not touch it, record its location and report it to the authorised supervisor. If the location might be subject to police or coronial process, do not disturb the object or the scene except as directed by that authority. Put in place an immediate stop-and-report route so that any worker who sees a sharp knows exactly what to do without having to decide. In training, create a reporting card that records the location, the people notified, the access controls in place and the specialist collection referral, without handling any real sharp.

instruction.heading: 5. Blood and bodily fluid exposure control
instruction.body: Blood and body-fluid contamination calls for an employer-approved exposure-control plan and a site-specific assessment by a competent person. Standard precautions apply to every such situation. The controls required depend on the setting, the materials involved, the extent of the contamination and the local rules that apply. No universal disinfectant strength, contact time, spray method or clearance claim can be taken from training material, and none is given here. Any treatment follows the product label and the employer's approved procedure, and a product's marketing does not authorise its use on a biological contamination. Where a worker has a possible exposure, the activity stops, the exposure response is started and a medical assessment is arranged through the employer's process. Compare scenarios by asking whether each one needs referral, additional evidence or an approved site procedure before anything else happens.

instruction.heading: 6. PPE selection, fit and removal
instruction.body: Personal protective equipment cannot replace hazard elimination, site controls or worker competence. It is selected from a documented risk assessment, must be compatible with the task and must fit the worker. Workers must not choose their own equipment from a supply cupboard. Incorrect removal, often called doffing, can cause self-contamination, so removal sequences are taught and checked by a qualified trainer in a controlled training environment, not improvised on a job. A worker who has been given an unfamiliar respirator without fit verification must stop until the suitability, fit, training and authorisation have been confirmed. In training, demonstrate checking the employer's selection records and requesting supervised competency verification, using training-only equipment.

instruction.heading: 7. Cleaning and disinfection boundaries
instruction.body: Removing visible soil, disinfecting and sterilising are three separate outcomes, and a job can achieve one without the others. An authorised procedure must identify the surface, device or material, any efficacy claim made for a product, the cleaning steps needed beforehand, the manufacturer's instructions and the limitations of the method. Inaccessible or damaged porous materials may need specialist handling. Visual inspection alone never establishes clearance. When a client asks for a 'fully disinfected' certificate after a surface has been wiped, the request is not supported by the work done. Decline the unsupported claim, explain that soil removal, disinfection and verification are different, and refer the verification question to the party with authority to make it. In training, audit a fictional work order for missing product approval, material compatibility and verification authority.

instruction.heading: 8. Porous surfaces and unsalvageable materials
instruction.body: Soft furnishings, underlays, timber joints and similar porous materials can keep contamination that cannot be seen on the surface. Decisions to retain, remove or dispose of such material must be taken by a competent, authorised person and must follow the property, insurance and waste controls that apply. Training must not prescribe intrusive treatment of unknown contamination. When a cleaner proposes a treatment for a potentially contaminated item, such as a mattress, the proposal needs specialist review first, because a method that moves material around or changes the contamination can make the position worse. Keep three questions apart in your decision memo: preservation of property, the risk evaluation, and the specialist disposal authorisation. In training, prepare a decision memo that separates those three questions for a fictional item.

instruction.heading: 9. Regulated waste identification and handoff
instruction.body: Waste descriptions and classifications vary between jurisdictions and between receiving facilities. Never assume that contaminated material belongs in general waste, and never assume that holding a cleaning qualification permits anyone to transport it. A compliant chain of custody can require licensed operators, suitable containers, labelling, manifests and an approved treatment destination. A contractor who offers to take bagged material in a private vehicle, without documentation, is offering something that lacks the authorised transport, the manifest, the approved destination and the consent of the responsible party. In training, complete a mock waste-handover form in which the classification is marked as pending, with the receiving party, the evidence and the unresolved approvals recorded.

instruction.heading: 10. Equipment segregation and transport
instruction.body: Reusable equipment can carry contaminants from one zone or site to another, and vehicles can carry them too. Equipment choice, handling, decontamination, storage and vehicle segregation need approved protocols and competent oversight. Do not improvise cleaning methods for contaminated tools, particularly powered or sensitive equipment, because an improvised method can damage the equipment or leave contamination behind. Before a piece of equipment used on a suspected contamination task is booked for another job, verify that it has been released through the documented process. A vacuum that was used on such a task and is scheduled straight afterwards for a domestic job needs that verification and a documented release before it is used again. In training, build a clean and dirty equipment inventory and an approval checkpoint list using fictional assets.

instruction.heading: 11. Incident reporting and exposure escalation
instruction.body: Needlestick injuries, splashes, skin contact and suspected inhalation exposures need prompt reporting and medical guidance under the employer's response procedure. Do not conceal an incident, and do not decide whether help is needed based on how you feel. A worker who feels well after a needlestick still needs to report it, because the need for medical guidance does not depend on symptoms. A worker who reports a possible splash to the mucous membranes and wants to finish the shift should be stopped from continuing, notified and referred for medical assessment. Document the time, the type of exposure, the first-response actions taken and the nominated occupational health contact, while protecting the worker's confidentiality. In training, rehearse a scripted incident notification and complete an anonymised exposure report template.

instruction.heading: 12. Verification, records and release boundaries
instruction.body: Job completion evidence must describe exactly what was authorised, what was done and what was inspected, together with the exclusions that remain and the sign-offs that were given. Photographs and the appearance of a surface do not validate microbiological safety. Clearance or any claim of unrestricted re-entry may be made only by a party that is competent and authorised under the applicable scheme. A property manager may demand an unconditional safety certificate while areas remain excluded. The correct response is a limited handover that states the authorised scope, what was done, the areas still excluded, the outcomes that are unverified and who can make any clearance claim. Never declare a scene medically or legally safe without the authority to do so. In training, review a fictional job file for missing approvals, incomplete scope records, excluded locations and unsupported claims.

instruction.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
instruction.body: Stop work and refer whenever any of the following is true: the biological hazard is uncertain or the contamination status is unverified; the required authorisation, release or competence is missing; the handling, transport, waste or exposure protocol is unknown; a sharp has been found or might be present; a worker may have been exposed; entry has been offered without written release; a party asks you to certify clearance or unrestricted re-entry. A stop-work decision is not a failure. Restart only after the authorised supervisor has documented the procedure and a qualified review has been completed.

procedure: Stop the activity and keep people out of the affected area.
Do not touch, move, sort, test or taste any unidentified material, and do not handle any sharp.
Notify the authorised supervisor immediately and record the time, the location, the people present and what was observed.
If anyone may have been exposed, follow the employer's exposure response, arrange medical assessment through the nominated process and do not self-treat beyond the employer's first-response steps.
Confirm the scope, the release and the authority in writing before any restart is considered.
Refer waste handling, specialist cleaning, decontamination and any clearance decision to the authorised party for that task.
Record the decision, the referral and the next competent party in the job file.
Issue a limited handover that states only what was done and what remains unresolved.

workedExamples.situation: An occupied apartment is described as needing 'just a deep clean' after a serious incident. The client wants a worker there tomorrow morning.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do before quoting or assigning anyone?
workedExamples.reasoning: Treat the description as unverified. Ask for an authorised site description and the written release from the responsible authority. Avoid entry until an appropriate supervisor has confirmed the scope. Record the request, the unknowns and the referral.

workedExamples.situation: A worker reports a needle-like object under debris while clearing a room.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the safest reporting and exclusion decision, and what must the worker not do?
workedExamples.reasoning: The worker must not handle or move the object. Stop work in that area, keep others out, report the location to the authorised supervisor and arrange specialist collection through the approved process. Record the location, the people notified and the access controls.

workedExamples.situation: A worker brings an unfamiliar respirator from the supply cupboard and says it looks right.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the worker able to start the task?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Suitability, fit, training and employer authorisation must be verified first. Self-selection is not an acceptable control, and the worker should request supervised competency verification.

workedExamples.situation: A worker reports a possible splash to the mouth during an assessment and wants to finish the shift and report later.
workedExamples.reasoning: End the activity and start the employer's exposure response. Arrange medical assessment through the nominated process. Delay in reporting is itself a failure of control, and the worker's wish to finish does not change the requirement.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks for a 'fully disinfected' certificate after the coordinator wiped one surface.
workedExamples.reasoning: Decline the certificate. Explain that a wipe does not establish disinfection or clearance, and that verification sits with the party authorised to make it. Record the request and the response.

workedExamples.situation: A contractor offers to take bagged material from the site in a private car, with no paperwork.
workedExamples.reasoning: The offer lacks authorised transport, a manifest, a receiving destination that is approved, labelling and container requirements, and the consent of the responsible party. Refuse the transfer and refer the handover to the authorised operator.

commonErrors.error: Accepting 'just a deep clean' as the scope of work after a serious incident.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat the description as unverified. Request the written site description, the release and the authority before quoting.

commonErrors.error: Treating a clean-looking surface or a photograph as proof that the area is safe.
commonErrors.prevention: State that appearance does not establish biological safety. Refer clearance to the authorised party.

commonErrors.error: Picking up or moving a sharp to see what it is.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not touch it. Stop, keep others out and report to the authorised supervisor.

commonErrors.error: Using a household product because the marketing says it kills everything.
commonErrors.prevention: Product use follows the label and the employer's approved procedure for that exact situation. Marketing does not authorise use.

commonErrors.error: Choosing respiratory or other PPE from the supply cupboard without a fit check or training.
commonErrors.prevention: Verify selection, fit, training and authorisation before any task starts.

commonErrors.error: Carrying contaminated bags home or to a depot in a private vehicle.
commonErrors.prevention: Refuse the transfer. Refer to the licensed waste handler with the documentation in place.

commonErrors.error: Reusing equipment from a suspected contamination task on another job straight away.
commonErrors.prevention: Hold the equipment until its release is documented through the approved process.

commonErrors.error: Waiting until the end of the shift to report a splash or needlestick.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, report at once and start the exposure response. Feeling well does not change the requirement to report.

commonErrors.error: Issuing an unconditional safety or clearance certificate while areas remain excluded.
commonErrors.prevention: Issue a limited handover that lists exclusions and unverified outcomes, and name who can make clearance claims.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This module does not grant authority to work on scenes, to enter affected premises or to carry out any regulated work. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or clearance.

Some work covered here is restricted to licensed, authorised or specially trained people, including trauma remediation, sharps collection, regulated waste transport and specialist decontamination. Verify with the relevant state or territory authority before any work is assigned.
Legal, police, coronial, insurer, property-owner and occupational-health authority must be obtained and recorded where it applies. Where the controlling authority is not identified, do not proceed.

They are not an Australia-wide statement. Australian equivalents: the duty to manage risk under the model WHS laws, enforced by the regulator in your state or territory, and the NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (document dated 2019).
Exposure management follows the employer's exposure-control plan and the local health guidance. The exposure response and medical evaluation are not replaced by this lesson.

No product name, strength, dilution, contact time or quantity is given in this lesson. Any product use follows the label and the approved procedure. Recipes and quantities for drug or chemical processing are not provided and are outside this module.
Biological safety and clearance decisions belong to competent, authorised parties. Photographs, surface appearance and a completed task do not establish that an area is safe.

summary: Biohazard and trauma work is a referral-first area. Ordinary cleaning practice does not transfer to it.
Uncertainty means stop and refer. Appearance, a photo or a finished wipe does not establish safety.
No entry without written release from every party that controls the site or holds authority over it.
Never touch an unidentified sharp. Stop, keep people out, report.
Report any exposure at once, regardless of symptoms, and follow the employer's exposure response.
PPE is selected, fitted and removed under documented procedure and training. It does not replace controls.
Soil removal, disinfection and clearance are separate outcomes. Only authorised parties make clearance claims.
Porous material and regulated waste need specialist decisions and licensed handling.
Record decisions, unknowns and referrals. Hand over only what was done, and state what remains unverified.

officialReferences.title: Duties of a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU)
officialReferences.covers: Confirms the PCBU duty to workers and others so far as reasonably practicable, and refers to the hierarchy of control. It does not say PPE is a last resort. Check your state or territory WHS regulator for the adopted law. Publisher: Safe Work Australia.

officialReferences.title: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (2019), CD34
officialReferences.pageDate: no page date shown; document dated 2019 (CD34)
officialReferences.covers: Read: sections on environmental cleaning, spills, hand hygiene, standard precautions and sharps. Not read: section 3.1.4 (reprocessing), 3.1.7 (waste), 4.1.2 (roles) and Appendix 6.1 (frequencies). Check those in the full PDF. Publisher: National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC).

officialReferences.title: Managing spills of blood and body fluids and substances
officialReferences.covers: Read through a summary tool (WebFetch): standard precautions and PPE for all spill cleaning; clear up the spill before cleaning the area and avoid aerosols; small spills wiped, then cleaned with detergent and warm water, with a hospital-grade disinfectant optional; sodium hypochlorite generally unnecessary; leak-proof bags for waste; the page advises against vinyl gloves for blood. Victorian guidance only.

officialReferences.title: Managing exposures to blood and body fluids or substances
officialReferences.covers: Read through a summary tool (WebFetch): first response after exposure (remove contaminated clothing, wash with soap and water, flush mucous membranes, rinse eyes gently, report immediately); medical evaluation with post-exposure prophylaxis offered as appropriate; document date, time, type and circumstances; each health service has a written protocol; outside a health service, see a general practitioner or the nearest emergency department. Victorian guidance only.

officialReferences.title: Cleaning and waste disposal procedures for infection control
officialReferences.covers: Read through a summary tool (WebFetch): regular cleaning of work areas, written cleaning protocols, standard precautions, avoiding aerosol-generating methods, single-use cloths where possible; spills of certain infectious materials need special procedures; three waste categories (general, clinical, pharmaceutical); clinical waste in yellow biohazard bags, sharps in approved containers, collection by licensed contractors. Victorian guidance only.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client says a flat needs 'just a deep clean' after a serious incident and offers keys today. What should the coordinator do first?
options: Quote the job and send a worker the same day to save time on the booking and the client's request
Pause, request written authority and site release, and avoid entry until the scope is confirmed.
Send the keys-holder's description to the worker as the work order for the flat today

knowledgeChecks.question: A photograph shows a clean-looking carpet beside a spill. What does this establish?
options: The area is clear for re-entry, since the carpet looks clean and no spill is visible now
Only the carpet edge needs checking, since the spill is near the middle of the room
Appearance does not establish biological safety, so the area is treated as unverified.

knowledgeChecks.question: A neighbour offers a contractor entry to a sealed property after an incident. What is missing?
options: A written release from the authority controlling the site and written authority from the responsible party.
A photograph of the front door taken from the footpath, which shows the lock and the frame are intact
A cup of tea with the neighbour, which gives them a chance to explain the incident and the keys

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker sees a needle-like object under debris. What is the correct immediate action?
options: Pick it up with gloves and bag it, since the gloves protect the hands from the sharp end
Stop, keep others out, do not handle the object and report it to the authorised supervisor.
Sweep it into a pile so it is out of the way while the rest of the debris is removed

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker reports a splash during a task and wants to finish the shift before reporting. What is the correct response?
options: Finish the shift and report at the end of the day, once the rest of the work is done
Rinse the area and continue the work if no symptoms appear over the next hour or so
Stop the activity, start the employer's exposure response and arrange medical assessment.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker picks a respirator from the supply cupboard without a fit check. What is the best response?
options: Stop until suitability, fit, training and authorisation are verified.
Accept it, because it is a respirator and looks like the right type
Check the fit only once a supervisor is on site to watch the process

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks for a 'fully disinfected' certificate after the coordinator wiped one surface. What is the best response?
options: Issue the certificate, since the surface was wiped and the wipe was done carefully by the coordinator today
Decline the unsupported claim and explain that soil removal, disinfection and verification are separate and need authority.
Issue a certificate for the wiped surface only, which is accurate because only that surface was touched by the wipe today

knowledgeChecks.question: A cleaner proposes steam cleaning a mattress that may be contaminated. What is the right step?
options: Steam it, because it is quick and the steam will kill anything on the surface straight away
Remove the cover only and keep the rest, so the mattress can be used again without much delay
Refer the proposal for specialist review before any treatment that could spread or change the contamination.

knowledgeChecks.question: A contractor offers to take bagged contaminated material in a private car with no paperwork. What is the assessment?
options: Refuse. Authorised transport, a manifest and an approved destination are missing.
Acceptable if the bags are sealed and the car is clean inside and out
Acceptable if you keep a receipt from the contractor for the job and the bags are tied

knowledgeChecks.question: A vacuum used on a suspected contamination task is booked for a domestic job straight afterwards. What is needed before it is reused?
options: A quick wipe over the outside, since the inside is clean if the bag is new
Verified decontamination and a documented equipment release before reuse.
Nothing, as long as the vacuum has a new bag fitted for the next job

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker feels well after a needlestick and asks whether they need to report it. What is the correct answer?
options: No. Feeling well means no report is needed, since the worker is not unwell at all
Only if bleeding is visible at the site, since a clean needle needs no report
Yes. Report promptly, because symptoms do not decide whether medical guidance is needed.

knowledgeChecks.question: A property manager demands an unconditional safety certificate while some areas remain excluded. What is appropriate?
options: Issue a limited handover that states scope, exclusions and unverified outcomes, and names who can make clearance claims.
Give a verbal assurance that the property is safe, since the manager has asked for a simple answer today
Sign an unconditional certificate to keep the client happy, since the manager is paying for the whole job
